title: What consistent really means
summary: Choose the guarantee for each operation and name what a partition changes.

steps.title: The balance and the activity list disagree
steps.text: A transfer succeeds. The balance screen shows the debit, but a refreshed activity list does not. Later, a refresh shows an even older list. These are different failures. A product can need a current balance, read-your-writes on confirmation, and monotonic reads while paging history without demanding the same guarantee everywhere.

steps.title: Separate time from transactions
steps.text: Write on client A and read before replication. Read-your-writes carries the writer’s floor. Client B alternates primary and replica reads so monotonic reads have a regression to prevent.

steps.title: Worked example: nobody is on call
steps.text: Two doctors each decide to go off call after reading the same snapshot. The writes touch different rows. Watch what row-level conflict checks leave behind.

rows.label: Write skew outcome
rows.how: Two snapshots see 2; each removes a different doctor

rows.label: Remote coordination floor
rows.how: 10 ms local path + 80 ms required RTT

rows.label: Session catch-up
rows.how: 300 writes/s × 2 s lag; a version token can require waiting

steps.q: A balance transaction is serializable. What does that alone establish about a later read from an asynchronous replica?
choices: It must include the transaction because the write was serializable
Its freshness still needs a read-routing or version guarantee
It is current once the replica reports that it is healthy
steps.why: Serializability orders transactions. It does not by itself make an asynchronous replica current.

steps.q: Why is saying our database is strongly consistent insufficient? Follow-up: choose guarantees for a reservation, save confirmation and public count.
checklist: Choose an atomic reservation, read-your-writes confirmation and stale public count
Explain overselling, a missing saved edit and tolerable stale counts
State which operations wait during a partition
steps.model: I need to know which operations, which replicas and which failure conditions that phrase covers. A last-seat reservation needs an atomic invariant, often a serializable transaction or conditional write. A save confirmation needs read-your-writes, perhaps by routing to an authority or waiting for a version. A public count can accept bounded staleness. During a partition I would defer the reservation, keep a local pending edit visible and label stale public data. The latency and availability costs differ by screen.

steps.title: Partitions and ordinary days
steps.text: On an ordinary day, stronger reads still pay for coordination, distance or waiting. During a partition, a node cannot both answer every request and guarantee the strongest view. Session guarantees can offer a narrower promise, such as seeing your own save. Define the required observation per operation and explain the degraded behavior instead of choosing one consistency label for the whole product.

diagram.label: A missing reply forces a choice
parts: The network may be slow or partitioned. A timeout cannot distinguish them.
Preserve the strong guarantee at the cost of availability.
Keep a weaker read path available and expose its freshness.

steps.q: Both doctors leave under snapshot isolation after reading the other as on call. Which remedy protects the roster invariant?
choices: Add optimistic version checks only to each doctor's own row
Lock each doctor's own row after reading both rows
Use serializable transactions with retries or a shared guard locked before checking
steps.why: The transactions update different rows. Own-row checks and locks do not serialize the shared roster check.

steps.q: Why not make every read linearizable? Follow-up: we have users an ocean away.
checklist: Calculate the illustrative 10 ms local path plus 80 ms remote trip
Choose a freshness bound for cached public summaries
Keep allocation decisions at a safe authority despite remote latency
steps.model: With the example's 10 ms local path and 80 ms remote trip, a required remote reply gives a rough 90 ms floor before queueing. Some protocols can serve safe local reads, but only under explicit lease, quorum or leadership rules. I would spend that coordination on decisions such as allocating money or stock, and avoid it for public summaries. The test is whether a stale result can cause harm and what the next action validates. A faster stale summary still needs a clear freshness promise.

steps.q: A partition isolates a region from the only seat-allocation authority. There are no preallocated regional rights. Which policy avoids overselling?
choices: Serve marked stale counts but defer exclusive seat claims
Accept local claims and reconcile duplicate seats after recovery
Accept claims while a cached count still shows available seats
steps.why: A stale count cannot allocate exclusive seats safely. Offline allocation would require a separate rights protocol.

takeaway: Ask which operation, which order and which failure, then choose the smallest sufficient guarantee.
